title: The genius of the octopus
text: One night in 2016, staff at the National Aquarium of New Zealand discovered that one of their residents had disappeared. Inky, a common octopus, had squeezed through a small gap at the top of his tank, crossed the floor and slipped into a narrow drainpipe that led directly to the sea. By the time anyone noticed, he was gone for good. For the people who worked with him, the escape was surprising, but not entirely unexpected. Octopuses, they said, are famous for being clever, curious and very hard to keep in one place.

In many ways, the octopus seems to come from another planet. It has three hearts, blue blood and no bones at all, which is why it can fit through any hole larger than its beak, the only hard part of its body. Even more remarkable is its nervous system. An octopus has around five hundred million neurons, roughly as many as a dog, but most of them are not in its head. Two thirds are found in its eight arms, which means that each arm can taste, touch and even make simple decisions on its own.

This unusual design allows the octopus to be a brilliant problem solver. In laboratories, octopuses have learnt to open jars to reach the crab inside, and some have even worked out how to unscrew the lid from the inside. In the wild, certain species collect coconut shells and carry them across the sea floor, later putting the two halves together to create a portable shelter. For a long time, scientists believed that only humans and a few other animals were capable of using tools in this way.

Octopuses are also masters of disguise. Their skin contains thousands of special cells that can change colour in less than a second, and they can even alter the texture of their skin to look like rock or seaweed. What makes this ability particularly puzzling is that most octopuses are thought to be colour blind. Researchers are still not sure how they manage to match their surroundings so perfectly, although one theory suggests that their skin itself may be able to detect light.

Perhaps the most entertaining stories, however, come from people who work with octopuses every day. Aquarium keepers describe animals that recognise individual people, squirt water at staff they do not like and switch off lights by aiming jets of water at them. In one well-known case, an octopus was found to be leaving its tank at night to visit a neighbouring tank, eat the fish and return home before morning.

Despite their intelligence, octopuses live surprisingly short lives. Most species survive for only one or two years, and females usually die soon after their eggs hatch. Some scientists believe this is one reason why their behaviour is so fascinating: unlike humans, they cannot learn from their parents, so almost everything they know must be discovered by themselves.

As for Inky, nobody knows what happened to him after his great escape. But his story travelled around the world, and it made many people look at these creatures differently. As one researcher put it, studying the octopus is the closest we may ever get to meeting an intelligent alien.

grammar.rule: Four parts like the Use of English paper of the Cambridge B2 First exam. Parts 2, 3 and 4: write your answers and press Check.

parts.title: Part 1 · Multiple-choice cloze
parts.help: Read the text and choose the word or phrase that best fits each gap.

parts.title: Part 2 · Open cloze
parts.help: Write one word in each gap.
parts.text: Octopuses are one of the {{6}} intelligent animals in the ocean. {{7}} dolphins and whales, they are not mammals, but they still show behaviour that is remarkably complex. Octopuses are also very good at hiding. When {{8}} feel threatened, they can release a cloud of dark ink, {{9}} confuses predators and gives them time to escape. Some species are even able to copy the shape of other animals, {{10}} as poisonous fish. It is no wonder that so {{11}} scientists find them fascinating.

parts.title: Part 3 · Word formation
parts.help: Use the word in capitals at the end of each gap to form a word that fits.
parts.text: The {{12}} of the octopus has amazed scientists for decades. In one famous {{13}}, an octopus learnt to open a jar {{14}} after watching another octopus do it. Their ability to change colour is also {{15}}. Some researchers think that octopuses could {{16}} us to understand how brains work better, and their {{17}} may one day help to design better robots.
